cards.title: 1.1 Shapes of simple molecules
body: Lewis structures of molecules show the shared electron pairs (bonding pairs) as short lines or as pair of dots between the atoms, and the unshared pairs or nonbonding pairs (or lone pairs) as pairs of dots on individual atoms.
Blow up all four balloons to the same size.
Electron pairs repel each other because they are like charges.
Electron pairs in the valence shell of an atom tend to orient themselves so that their total energy is minimized.
Repulsive force decreases with an increase of inter-pair angle.

cards.title: 1.1 Shapes of simple molecules
body: Draw Lewis structures for O₂ and F₂. How many bonding pairs? How many lone pairs on each F in F₂?
Peek
O₂: double bond (2 shared pairs), 2 lone pairs on each O. F₂: single bond, 3 lone pairs on each F. Lewis drawings are flat; real molecules are 3-D — that is why we need VSEPR.

cards.title: VSEPR in one breath
body: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion: electron pairs around a central atom push apart and sit as far from each other as they can.
*Electron-pair geometry* counts **all** pairs (bonds + lone pairs). *Molecular shape* counts only atoms (lone pairs still push, but you don’t “see” them in the shape name).

cards.title: 2 pairs → linear
body: 180°. BeH₂, CO₂. All atoms in a straight line.

cards.title: 3 pairs → trigonal planar
body: 120°. BF₃. Flat triangle.

cards.title: 4 pairs → tetrahedral
body: 109.5°. CH₄. Central atom in the middle of a pyramid with a triangular base.

cards.title: Lone pairs change the name
body: H₂O: 4 pairs (2 bond + 2 lone) → electron geometry tetrahedral, *shape bent* (~104.5°). NH₃: 3 bond + 1 lone → *trigonal pyramidal*.

cards.title: If every pair is a bond, shape name = electron-pair name.
Mnemonic — lone pairs are bullies
body: Lone pair–lone pair repulsion > lone pair–bond pair > bond–bond. That is why water is squeezed from 109.5° to about 104.5°.
Why it matters: if H₂O were linear it would not be a liquid at room temperature — polarity (and life) depends on the bent shape.

cards.title: 1.2 Crystals
body: A **crystal** is a solid whose particles sit in a repeating 3-D pattern. That pattern is the **crystal lattice**. The smallest repeating box that still has the full symmetry is the **unit cell**.
**Coordination number** = how many nearest neighbours touch a particle. In NaCl each Na⁺ has 6 Cl⁻ neighbours (and vice versa).
Seven crystal systems (by unit-cell edge lengths and angles): cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, hexagonal, trigonal (rhombohedral), monoclinic, triclinic.

units.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
units.intro: Organic chemistry = chemistry of carbon compounds (plus H, and often O, N, X…). Carbon has 4 valence electrons → four bonds, long chains, rings, single / double / triple bonds.

cards.title: Organic vs inorganic
body: Organic: covalent, often low m.p., burn to CO₂ + H₂O, may show isomerism. Inorganic: often ionic, high m.p., no typical combustion to CO₂.

cards.title: 2.1.1 Introduction
body: Until the early 19th century, chemists had managed to make many simple compounds in the laboratory, but were still unable to produce the complex molecules that they found in living organisms.
From this, the idea that there was a “vital force” in the formation of organic compounds was developed.
One consequence of this vital force, chemists believed, was that organic compounds could not be prepared and manipulated in the laboratory as inorganic compounds could.
In 1928, Friedrich Wohler discovered that it was possible to convert the inorganic salt ammonium cyanate into the organic substance urea, which had previously been found in human urine.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Some Differences between Organic and Inorganic Compounds
body: Although organic compounds are governed by the same laws that apply to inorganic compounds, their properties can sometimes be quite different from those of inorganic compounds.
The number of known organic compounds is in the millions, while that of inorganic compounds is in the hundreds of thousands.
All organic compounds are made of carbon.
Carbon is a unique non-metal found in group IV of the Periodic Table.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Classification of Organic Compounds
body: In a very broad sense organic compounds can be divided into two groups: those that have an open-chain structure and those that are cyclic or their structures include rings.
Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with organic molecules.
Plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide in the air into organic compounds through the process of photosynthesis.
Animals and other organisms then feed on plants to obtain their own organic compounds.

Chemical Bonding and Formulas of Hydrocarbons A carbon atom is tetravalent or always forms four bonds.
In organic chemistry, organic molecules are, most of the time, represented by using molecular formula, structural formula or condensed structural formula.

cards.title: 2.2.2 The Alkanes Series
body: The alkane series comprises the simplest aliphatic hydrocarbons.
The general formula of the alkane series is CnH2n+2, where n = 1, 2, 3, etc.
All side branches are called substituent groups, because they appear as a substitute for a hydrogen atom in the straight chain.

cards.title: 2.2.3 The Alkenes Series
body: A basic principle of the IUPAC system is that the functional groups are to be given a preferred status in the naming of a compound.
The different types of isomerism shown by alkenes are: skeletal or chain isomerism, position isomerism, and geometric or cis-trans isomerism.
A set of alkenes with the same formula may have the same number of carbon atoms in their skeleton, but the location of either the double bond or the substituents attached to the skeleton may differ.

cards.title: 2.2.4 The Alkynes Series
body: Many of the alkynes are used to synthesize other chemical products.
The raw materials that are needed to make acetylene are calcium carbonate and coal.
An important use of acetylene is in oxyacetylene gas welding.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Aromatic Compounds
body: The term “aromatic” was originally used because many of the benzene-related compounds known in the 19th century were found in pleasant-smelling (aroma) oils that came from spices, fruits and other plant parts.
Benzene itself and other organic compounds that contain benzene rings as part of their structure are called aromatic compounds, whether they have odour or not.
In 1865 the German chemist, Friedrick August Kekule, proposed a different kind of structure for benzene: a hexagon of carbon atoms with alternating single and double bonds.

cards.q: What is the systematic IUPAC name for the branched alkane with the formula $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Find the longest continuous carbon chain**
The chain has four carbon atoms, so the parent name is **butane**.

**Step 2: Number the parent chain**
Number from left to right to give the methyl substituent the lowest possible number:
$$\text{C}_1(\text{CH}_3)-\text{C}_2\text{H(CH}_3)-\text{C}_3\text{H}_2-\text{C}_4\text{H}_3$$
This places the methyl branch at carbon-2. Numbering from right to left would place it at carbon-3, which is incorrect.

**Step 3: Assemble the IUPAC name**
Combining the substituent position with the parent chain yields **2-methylbutane**.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The systematic name is **2-methylbutane**.

cards.title: 2.3 Derivatives — functional groups
body: **Soaps** = sodium / potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids (from fats + NaOH). They have a ionic head (loves water) and a hydrocarbon tail (loves grease) — that is why they lift dirt. **Soapless detergents** work in hard water where soap forms scum.

tips.text: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with organic molecules.
An organic molecule is one that contains carbon.
Plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide in the air into organic compounds through the process of photosynthesis.

One important group of organic compounds is the hydrocarbons. These molecules contain carbon and hydrogen atoms only, which can be arranged in simple or complex chains and rings.
Almost all organic compounds are considered as derivatives of hydrocarbons.

body: X-ray machines have now been connected to computers in the development of machines called CAT scanners.
Medical procedures using radiation have saved thousands of lives through the detection and treatment of conditions ranging from hyperthyroidism to bone cancer.

cards.q: What is the primary factor that dictates the stability of a given atomic nucleus?

options.A: The density of the electron cloud
options.B: The chemical state of the atom
options.C: The neutron-to-proton ($$n/p$$) ratio in the nucleus
options.D: The volume of the unit cell

cards.why:
**Step 1: Review nuclear force relationships**
Nuclear stability is determined by the balance between the attractive strong nuclear force (primarily from neutrons and protons) and the repulsive electrostatic force (between protons).

**Step 2: Identify the critical ratio**
This balance is dictated by the ratio of neutrons to protons ($$n/p$$) in the nucleus. Deviations from the stable ratio lead to instability and decay.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The stability is dictated by **The neutron-to-proton ($$n/p$$) ratio in the nucleus**.

The Becquerel (Bq) is the official SI unit for measuring radioactivity, where $$1\text{ Bq} = 1\text{ disintegration per second}$$.

The standard SI unit is **Becquerel (Bq)**.

cards.title: 3.7.1 Radioactive Wastes
body: Low-level waste: waste that is only slightly radioactive and gives off small amounts of radiation.
Because it emits only small amounts of radiation, low-level waste is usually sealed in steel drums and buried at special sites.
For example, a large percentage of high-level waste from commercial nuclear power plants comes from used or spent nuclear fuel that has released much of its energy.
While storage onsite has been environmentally safe, what is needed today is a permanent disposal site, or repository, for existing and future high-level waste.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following materials is most effective at blocking highly penetrating gamma ($$\gamma$$) radiation?

options.B: A thin layer of aluminum foil
options.C: A thick block of lead or heavy concrete

cards.why:
**Step 1: Evaluate gamma ray characteristics**
Gamma rays are massless, uncharged photons with extreme penetrating power, meaning they can easily pass through light, low-density materials like paper, wood, or aluminum.

**Step 2: Identify effective shielding**
To absorb gamma rays effectively, materials with extremely high densities and high atomic numbers (like lead or heavy concrete) are required to absorb the photon energy.

**Step 3: Final Result**
**A thick block of lead or heavy concrete** is most effective.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which nuclear process is currently harnessed in commercial nuclear power plants worldwide to generate electricity?

options.B: Controlled nuclear fission of heavy isotopes

cards.why:
**Step 1: Review current nuclear power technology**
Commercial nuclear power plants utilize the heat generated from nuclear reactions to produce steam and electricity.

**Step 2: Identify the reaction type**
Currently, commercial reactors rely exclusively on the controlled nuclear fission of heavy, splitable isotopes (primarily Uranium-235). Controlled fusion has not yet been commercialized.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The process used is **Controlled nuclear fission of heavy isotopes**.
